# QnA Bots
All right, let's start with LLMs as a Q&A bot. If you think about LLMs when they first came in the first GPT 3.5, which was really mind-blowing, you would get a question and you would get an answer. Now, how would this interaction happen on a terminal, on a client-server interaction, where this communication happens by an HTTP protocol?

What are the first principles that govern the HTTP relationship between a client and the server? The first thing that we need to understand is that the client-server interaction with a client is stateless, so any follow-up interactions that you're having on top of this are something that's contained by the client. Okay, with that statement, I think I am making myself clear on where I'm heading, and I hope it may become abundantly clear what the idea behind the API is. 

The first thing we could think of is that, because every subsequent message needs to, because these are stateless interactions, one question can only be answered once. Once that interaction transaction happens, the server does not know anything about your Q&A answers. The next time you send a question and an answer, the message starts from scratch. The server starts from scratch, and it takes your client interactions as a new interaction. It does not remember anything about your client state. Remember, I am talking about old interactions. A lot of these modern systems now have a lot of session and state management principles, but we are not concerned about that right now. We are only concerned about what are LLMs' capabilities that made us interact with them, okay, great.

The next step of this evolution is that, when we send multiple messages, that's a turn. One user interaction followed by a 1:1 user response is one set of turns. That's the standard jargon around it. The second jargon that you should be aware of is what happens. How do you interact after that interaction? How do you interact after that happens? You do that by you, the client, passing more information after you have shared your initial list, and that's how JSON will come into the picture, because you send out a string of text. You get a response, which is in a JSON format. In the next interaction, for the server, you send out both the user's previous message and the previous system response, which is now called an assistant response, and then the new user message. Essentially, you are asking the server to continue this conversation after you have had the previous conversations. That is how the server right now knows your LLMQA bot. 

We now move to one part of the interaction that we are dealing with. The other thing is that we have now done subsequent QnA bots. - Remind me if today is my anniversary.

That was the sole purpose of tool calls.

This may not seem like a huge deal, like, "What's the huge deal?" No, there is a very clear idea which is hiding in plain sight. Tools are just functions written by you to execute, but they did not give them the power to execute those functions. LLMs, right now after that Q&A evolution, have just reached the point of, "Hey, you need to use this XYZ tool right now." The moment you hit this XYZ tool, how do you execute that tool? That entire process of execution is called an "hardness." That's something that you need to understand in this process. That is what an agentic hardness looks like, okay, I think. 


We finally understand what a harness is and give more examples of what a harness is. Think of a harness like the LLM selects the tool called "how you executed", which is what the harness is about. The harness is supposed to return the results of the tool call selected by the LLM back to the LLM so that the LLM can have a composite response.
Let me break it down again:
1. You ask a question.
2. You get a response.
3. You ask another follow-up question.
4. You get a set of tools from which you need to select the LLM.
5. The LLM selects the tool, passes it on to the harness.
6. The harness executes it and returns it back to the LLM.

# What are Agents

I feel that we have talked enough about what hooks are and what tools are, with sufficient demonstration. I would like now to move to what an agent is. I like to define an agent as a client-side loop. An agent is a client-side state machine where the LLM is placed inside an autonomous loop. Instead of answering a question and answering in a single term or in a multi-term, the system evaluates the user's goals and determines the sequence of actions. It evaluates the outcomes of these actions via the harness and loops until the objective is met.

In very, very simple terms, an agent by itself is a loop. It does a lot of things, which tool calls. One of those tool calls is I would not like to go into the codex journey, because the codex journey is huge by itself. Instead, what I would like to focus more on is how the loop works? If you define one class of loop, which is with the harness, you call an LLM. It gets a tool response, and then it closes when it's finally able to churn that to the right. Right now, an agent is a superset of that harness, multiple harnesses, so it's not going to work with just one harness by itself. It's going to work with multiple harnesses, and in the end, whatever user asks as a question, the answer gets returned.
